idiom_name: java.util.stream pipeline (Stream.filter/map/reduce) with a terminal operation
implementation_notes: The JDK's Stream API is the fusion mechanism: intermediate operations are always lazy and compose into a stream pipeline that ends in exactly one terminal operation, so filtering, mapping and summing can be fused into a single pass with minimal intermediate state, and nothing is materialized unless a collector or toList asks for it. Streams are consumed once, are pipeline-shaped from source to sink, and short-circuiting operations (limit, findFirst, anyMatch) can end the traversal early on unbounded sources. The classic pre-Java-8 forms - an Iterator chain or a hand-written loop - remain the fallback when the pipeline is short, and IntStream/LongStream/DoubleStream remove boxing from numeric stages.
pitfalls: A stream is consumed once: reusing it - or returning it from a method and streaming it twice - throws IllegalStateException.

Stateful or side-effecting lambdas (mutating a shared list, logging per element, using peek to do the real work) break the fusion guarantees, change results under parallel streams, and peek may not be invoked for elements the pipeline short-circuits past.
A stream is lazy until its terminal operation: building one without terminating it (or terminating it inside a loop) silently repeats the source traversal.
